analysis.one_liner: Bans states from regulating wireless phone rates and entry, replacing state rules with one federal consumer standard.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote, with no cosponsors; state authority over wireless rates remained in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Communications Act to stop state and local governments from regulating or adjudicating the rates charged by, and the entry of, wireless phone providers. In its place, the Federal Communications Commission would have had one year to write a single national set of customer service and consumer protection rules for wireless companies. The bill never got a hearing, never got a vote, and never left the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Wireless carriers, and their investors, would benefit most. States today can regulate the rates wireless companies charge and challenge new fees or terms; the bill would have taken that authority away and replaced it with a single federal rule written by the FCC. National carriers would deal with one set of standards instead of many state ones, and would face no state-level rate limits at all. Consumers would get whatever protections the FCC chose to write, and nothing more.
analysis.who_benefits_short: National wireless carriers and their investors

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit state and local governments from regulating or adjudicating the entry of, or the rates charged by, providers of commercial or private mobile service, closing off the existing state authority that current law preserves. [S3]

The FCC would be required to adopt a final rule within one year establishing customer service and consumer protection requirements for wireless providers, with the state preemption taking effect 180 days after that rule. [S3]
A single national standard would replace a patchwork of state rules, which wireless companies argue reduces compliance costs across the roughly 50 markets in which they operate. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who rely on state-level protection. If a state wanted to cap wireless rates, challenge a price increase, or stop a carrier from overcharging customers, this bill would bar it from doing so. Consumers would depend entirely on whatever the FCC chose to include in its rule, and a federal rulemaking can take years to produce and enforce.

drawbacks.text: Preempting state rate and entry regulation removes the most direct tool states have against wireless overcharges, and the federal consumer protection rule in the bill is a promise, not a guarantee: the FCC would be free to write weak requirements, and its rule could be weakened or repealed by later commissions. [S3]

The bill's customer service standards would apply only through FCC rulemaking, so between enactment and the final rule (up to 18 months, at minimum) consumers would have no new protections even as their state protections were scheduled to lapse. [S3]

Supporters of state authority would also note that states can move faster than a federal agency when a local market problem, such as unauthorized charges or deceptive billing in a specific state, needs to be stopped. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade the bill offered was a single federal standard in exchange for the elimination of state rate and entry regulation. For carriers that is clearly a gain. For consumers it is a gamble: their protections would hinge entirely on one future FCC rule, while their strongest existing remedy, a state rate law or state court action, would be gone. On balance the bill's consumer title looks thin next to the preemption title it enables, and with no cosponsors it drew no visible support in the Senate.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended; the committee never acted on it and no vote was ever held.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Pryor introduced the bill on October 16, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. [S1]
The committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing or a vote and expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, states kept their authority to regulate wireless rates and entry, and consumers kept whatever state-level remedies existed; wireless carriers did not get the federal preemption they would have gained. Nobody acted to move the bill, so the status quo won by default.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and consumers kept existing authority

for.name: Sen. Mark Pryor (D-AR)
for.role: Sponsor; member of the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call or committee votes were ever taken, and with zero cosponsors the bill's support in the Senate is unrecorded beyond its sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have barred every state and local government from regulating or adjudicating wireless rates and entry, and would have replaced state consumer rules with a single FCC standard. Carriers would face no state rate limits at all, and consumers would depend entirely on whatever the FCC chose to write. The bill died, so nothing changed.

The bill would strip state and local governments of their existing authority under the Communications Act to regulate wireless rates and adjudicate disputes with carriers, taking away a tool states use on behalf of their residents.
